extracted.intended_audience: scientific inquirers, philosophers of science, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing, evaluating, and explaining empirical (derivative) laws versus ultimate laws of causation, including signs that a law is derivative and limits on generalization. Applies to analysis of causal sequences, progressive effects, and the proper use of observational methods and deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an empirical law
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific inquirers give the name of Empirical Laws to those uniformities which observation or experiment has shown to exist, but on which they hesitate to rely in cases varying much from those which have been actually observed, for want of seeing any reason why such a law should exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An empirical law is a derivative law whose derivation is not yet known; to state its explanation would be to state the ultimate causes on which it is contingent. Examples: local tidal laws, meteorological sequences, certain chemical generalizations. Empirical laws require deduction or experimental confirmation to be accepted beyond observed cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit generalizations of empirical laws to observed scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws can only be received as true within the limits of time and place in which they have been found true by observation; and not merely the limits of time and place, but of time, place, and circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because empirical laws may depend on particular collocations of agents (which have no general law), one should not extend them beyond the conditions actually observed without trial. Example: coal-bed stratification on Earth cannot be assumed on other planets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish uniform succession from causation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a phenomenon goes on increasing, or periodically increases and diminishes, or goes through any continued and unceasing process of variation reducible to a uniform rule or law of succession, we do not on this account presume that any two successive terms of the series are cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat successive stages (e.g., spring then summer) as cause and effect; instead seek underlying continuous causes or common antecedents. The conditional but invariable antecedent is not necessarily the cause unless it is the unconditional antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement alone does not prove causation
rubrics_metrics.description: No generalization amounts to more than an empirical law when the only proof on which it rests is that of the Method of Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method of Agreement can only ascertain the whole of the circumstances common to all observed cases but cannot determine which of those common circumstances is the true cause; results based solely on it remain empirical until corroborated by Method of Difference or deductive explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require Method of Difference or deduction to establish causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The utmost that the Method of Agreement can do is to ascertain the aggregate of common circumstances; none of them can be received in any other character than that of derivative laws, until either confirmed by the Method of Difference, or explained deductively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To elevate an empirical uniformity to a law of causation (or to discover ultimate causes), perform controlled contrasts (Method of Difference) or produce a deductive account from more fundamental laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of deductions by empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The verification of a deduction usually consists in the comparison of its results with empirical laws previously ascertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical generalizations as tests for deductions derived from proposed ultimate laws; agreement increases credibility, but attention must be paid to whether the empirical laws themselves are derivative or contingent on collocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign: presence of intermediate links implies a derivative law
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sign is, if between the antecedent a and the consequent b there be evidence of some intermediate link; some phenomenon of which we can surmise the existence, though ... we are unable to ascertain its precise nature and laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an intermediate phenomenon x is plausible (e.g., corpuscular processes in chemistry or physiology), then a→b is likely resolvable into a→x and x→b; treat observed law as derivative and search for intermediate mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign: extremely complex antecedent indicates derivability
rubrics_metrics.description: The second is, when the antecedent is an extremely complex phenomenon, and its effects, therefore, probably in part at least, compounded of the effects of its different elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex antecedents (homogeneous or heterogeneous aggregates) usually mean the observed sequence is composed of parts' effects. Examples: the weight of a body (sum of particle weights) and meteorological barometric changes (air + vapor). Favor analysis into component causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative laws often depend on collocation of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative laws ... mostly depend on those ultimate laws, and an ultimate fact; namely, the mode of co-existence of some of the component elements of the universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many derivative regularities require not only laws but particular combinations (collocations) of agents; because collocations have no known general principle, derivative laws depending on them are less generalizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws vary in authority according to presumed resolvability
rubrics_metrics.description: These empirical laws may be of greater or less authority, according as there is reason to presume that they are resolvable into laws only, or into laws and collocations together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess strength of an empirical law by whether evidence suggests it arises from single causes (stronger) or from collocations (weaker). Use experimental or deductive work to discriminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive effects arise from composition of successive causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause which continues in action must on a strict analysis be considered as a number of causes exactly similar, successively introduced, and producing by their combination the sum of the effects which they would severally produce if they acted singly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat continuous causes producing progressive effects as a series of instantaneous contributions (use calculus/deduction where appropriate). Examples: rusting, gravitational acceleration as sum of infinitesimal increments; such cases are best treated deductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: When cause changes progressively, expect unequal and qualitative changes in effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When the cause does not merely continue in action, but undergoes, during the same time, a progressive change ... the total effect goes on accumulating by the continual addition of a fresh effect to that already produced, but ... the quantities added are unequal, and even the quality may now be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze combined effects of continuance and progressive change of causes (e.g., seasonal temperature changes, planetary motion). Model as double series and anticipate periodical or complex behaviors arising from interactions and reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of empirical laws to distinguish
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of empirical laws: those known to be laws of causation, but presumed to be resolvable into simpler laws; and those not known to be laws of causation at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both kinds demand deductive explanation and serve to verify deductions; prioritize uncovering underlying laws or intermediate links to move from mere empirical regularity to causal understanding.
